title: Earth-Moon-Sun: Scale, Eclipses and Tides
description: Relative sizes and distances, how solar and lunar eclipses occur.
content_html:
Putting the Solar System to Scale

Before we can understand eclipses and tides we need to appreciate the vast differences in size and distance between Earth, Moon and Sun. The Sun has a mean diameter of approximately 1.4 million km — about 109 times wider than Earth. The Moon, with its mean diameter of ~3 500 km, is only about 1/400th of the Sun’s diameter. Yet by a remarkable cosmic coincidence the Moon is also roughly 1/400th of the distance from Earth to the Sun. This near-perfect size-to-distance ratio means the Moon’s angular diameter as seen from Earth is almost identical to the Sun’s angular diameter (both roughly 0.5°). This coincidence is what makes total solar eclipses possible.

Key Fact

Sun diameter: ~1.4 million km. Earth diameter: ~13 000 km. Moon diameter: ~3 500 km. Earth–Moon distance: ~384 000 km. Earth–Sun distance: ~150 million km (1 AU). The Moon and Sun have nearly equal angular diameters (~0.5°) as seen from Earth.

Solar Eclipses: Three Types

A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes in front of the Sun as seen from Earth. Because both the Moon’s orbit and the Moon’s size are not perfectly constant, three distinct types of solar eclipse are possible.

In a total solar eclipse, the Moon is at the right distance (close enough in its elliptical orbit) that it completely covers the Sun’s photosphere. The sky darkens dramatically, the solar corona becomes visible, and totality can last up to about 7 minutes. Observers must be inside the Moon’s umbra — the region of total shadow where no direct sunlight reaches. The path of totality is only around 100–250 km wide, but millions of people in the surrounding penumbra (partial shadow) see a partial solar eclipse.

In a annular solar eclipse, the Moon is near apogee (its farthest point from Earth) and therefore appears slightly smaller in angular size than the Sun. It cannot completely cover the Sun’s disc, leaving a bright ring — the annulus — of sunlight visible around the Moon’s silhouette. A partial solar eclipse occurs in the penumbral region surrounding any solar eclipse.

The Moon’s orbital plane is tilted about 5° relative to Earth’s orbital plane (the ecliptic). Most new moons therefore pass a little above or below the Sun in the sky and cast their shadow into space above or below Earth. Solar eclipses only occur when a new moon happens near one of the two nodes — the intersection points where the Moon’s orbit crosses the ecliptic. This restricts total solar eclipses to just a few per decade at any given location.

Lunar Eclipses: Total and Partial

A lunar eclipse occurs when Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon, casting its shadow across the Moon’s surface. Earth’s shadow has two zones: the central umbra (complete shadow) and the surrounding penumbra (partial shadow).

During a total lunar eclipse, the entire Moon enters Earth’s umbra. The Moon does not disappear entirely — it often glows deep red or copper as Earth’s atmosphere refracts and scatters sunlight inward, redirecting mostly red wavelengths onto the lunar surface. This is the same Rayleigh scattering that colours sunsets. The progression of a total lunar eclipse is described by four umbral contact points:

  • First umbral contact (U1) — the Moon’s limb first touches the edge of the umbra; the partial phase begins.
  • Second umbral contact (U2) — the Moon is fully within the umbra; totality begins.
  • Third umbral contact (U3) — the Moon’s limb first re-emerges from the umbra; totality ends.
  • Fourth umbral contact (U4) — the Moon fully leaves the umbra; the partial phase ends.

In a partial lunar eclipse, only part of the Moon enters Earth’s umbra, and only a dark ‘bite’ appears on the Moon’s surface. Lunar eclipses — unlike solar eclipses — are visible from the entire night-side hemisphere of Earth simultaneously, which is why any given observer sees more total lunar eclipses than total solar eclipses during a lifetime.

Tides: The Differential Gravity Explanation

Many students make a critical error when explaining tides: they think of the Moon pulling the nearest ocean toward it like a magnet. This explains only one tidal bulge — but there are two high tides per day on Earth. To understand both bulges we need differential gravity.

Exam reports consistently identify this as one of the most common errors. A single Moon-pull can only produce one oceanic bulge on the near side. But the far side of Earth is further from the Moon and experiences a weaker gravitational pull than the solid Earth beneath it. From Earth’s frame of reference, the far-side ocean is effectively ‘left behind’, forming the second bulge. Earth’s rotation then carries any location through both bulges in roughly 24 hours, producing two high tides and two low tides per day.

The Sun also exerts a tidal influence on Earth’s oceans, roughly 46% as strong as the Moon’s despite the Sun’s far greater mass (its much greater distance reduces its differential gravitational effect). When the Moon and Sun pull in the same direction — at new moon and full moon — their tidal effects add together to produce spring tides: unusually high high tides and unusually low low tides. When the Moon and Sun are at right angles to Earth (at first and last quarter), their tidal pulls partially cancel, producing neap tides: smaller tidal range with less difference between high and low tide.

Key Fact

Spring tides occur at new moon and full moon (Moon-Earth-Sun aligned); neap tides occur at first and last quarter (Moon-Earth-Sun at 90°). Earth’s rotation carries each location through two tidal bulges approximately every 24 hours, producing two high tides and two low tides daily.
exam_tip_html: For eclipse questions, label every element of any diagram you draw: umbra, penumbra, positions of Moon/Earth/Sun, and the observer’s location. For the eclipse type, remember that a total solar eclipse requires the Moon to be near perigee (close enough to cover the Sun); an annular eclipse occurs near apogee (too small to cover). For tides, the key examiner note is that you must explain both tidal bulges — the near-side bulge (Moon’s direct pull) AND the far-side bulge (Earth is pulled more than the far-side ocean, leaving it behind). One bulge alone is never enough for full marks. For spring vs neap, remember: spring = straight line (new/full moon); neap = right angle (quarter phases).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Sun (diameter ~1.4 million km) and Moon (~3 500 km diameter) have nearly equal angular diameters (~0.5°) as seen from Earth, making total solar eclipses possible. Three types of solar eclipse exist: total, partial and annular.
  • Lunar eclipses are described by four umbral contact points (U1–U4). During totality the Moon appears red because Earth’s atmosphere refracts red sunlight onto the lunar surface.
  • Tides arise from differential gravity: both the near-side and far-side tidal bulges must be explained to account for two high tides per day. Spring tides (new/full moon) have the greatest range; neap tides (quarter moons) have the smallest range.

practice_questions.text:
During which phase of the Moon do spring tides occur?
A) First and last quarter
B) New moon only
C) New moon and full moon
D) Full moon only
practice_questions.marks: C) New moon and full moon [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the approximate mean diameter of the Sun.
practice_questions.marks: 1.4 million km (accept 1 390 000 km to 1 400 000 km) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between the umbra and the penumbra of a shadow.
practice_questions.marks: The umbra is the region of total shadow where no direct sunlight reaches [1]; the penumbra is the region of partial shadow surrounding the umbra, where some sunlight is still visible [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain why an observer in the umbra sees a total solar eclipse, while an observer in the surrounding penumbra sees only a partial solar eclipse.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States that the umbra is the region of complete shadow where the Moon fully blocks all direct sunlight [1]; an observer here sees the Moon completely covering the Sun's photosphere — a total eclipse [1]; in the penumbra only part of the Sun is blocked by the Moon, so observers see a partially covered Sun — a partial eclipse [1].
Secure: Correct explanation of one region and one eclipse type.
Developing: Mentions umbra/penumbra without clear link to eclipse type.
Emerging: Vague or incorrect.

practice_questions.text: Caerwyn Observatory is running a public lecture on tides. The presenter asks the audience why there are two high tides per day. A student replies: 'The Moon's gravity pulls the ocean on the side nearest to the Moon, creating a tidal bulge.' Evaluate this answer, explaining what is correct and what is missing.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correct element — the Moon's gravitational attraction does produce a bulge on the near side [1]; what is missing: the student has not accounted for the second bulge on the far side [1]; the far-side bulge occurs because the Moon pulls Earth's solid body more strongly than the far-side ocean — from Earth's reference frame, the far-side ocean is 'left behind', forming a second bulge [1]; Earth's rotation carries each location through both bulges in approximately 24 hours, producing two high tides per day [1].
Secure: Identifies the missing far-side explanation and gives a partial mechanism.
Developing: Notes there are two tides but cannot explain the far-side bulge.
Emerging: No credit-worthy content.

practice_questions.text:
A member of the Brackenfell Observing Society has just witnessed a partial lunar eclipse from Cumbria. She recorded the following times: first umbral contact at 22:15, and the Moon beginning to leave the umbra at 23:47.

Describe fully what she would have observed during this sequence. In your answer explain why the Moon does not disappear completely during the partial phase, and why observers across the whole of the night-side of Earth can see a lunar eclipse simultaneously.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Describes the partial eclipse — a curved dark shadow (Earth's umbral shadow) progressively covering part of the Moon's disc from 22:15 [1]; the dark portion is Earth's umbra and the observer would see the boundary between lit and dark parts of the Moon as a curved arc (the shape of Earth's shadow, confirming Earth is spherical) [1]; the Moon does not disappear completely because only part of it enters the umbra — the rest remains in the penumbra or sunlight [1]; even the umbral portion is not entirely dark because Earth's atmosphere refracts some red/orange sunlight into the umbra — but in a partial eclipse this effect is subtle since not all of the Moon is in the umbra [1]; lunar eclipses are visible from the entire night-side hemisphere of Earth simultaneously because Earth is casting a shadow away from the Sun — any observer on the night side has an unobstructed view of the Moon entering Earth's shadow [1]; contrasts with solar eclipses which are only visible along a narrow path [1].
Secure (3-4): Correct description of the partial eclipse sequence and explanation of simultaneous visibility.
Developing (1-2): One or two relevant facts without full development.
Emerging (0): No credit-worthy content.

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of solar eclipse occurs when the Moon is at apogee and appears slightly smaller than the Sun?
What is the name for the unusually large tidal range that occurs when the Moon, Earth and Sun are aligned?
Second umbral contact (U2) marks the moment when the Moon is ___ within Earth's umbra.
The far-side tidal bulge forms because Earth is pulled ___ the far-side ocean by the Moon's gravity.
Match each alignment of Moon, Earth and Sun to the correct tidal type:
left: Moon-Earth-Sun in a straight line (new/full moon)
Moon at 90° to Earth-Sun line (quarter phase)
right: Total solar eclipse possible if nodes align

flashcard_questions.q: What is the approximate mean diameter of the Sun?
flashcard_questions.a: Approximately 1.4 million km — about 109 times Earth's diameter.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is the angular diameter of the Moon and Sun nearly equal as seen from Earth?
flashcard_questions.a: The Moon is ~400 times smaller than the Sun but also ~400 times closer, making their apparent sizes nearly equal.

flashcard_questions.q: What is an annular solar eclipse?
flashcard_questions.a: A solar eclipse when the Moon is near apogee and too small to fully cover the Sun, leaving a ring of sunlight visible.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the four umbral contact points of a lunar eclipse?
flashcard_questions.a: U1 (Moon enters umbra), U2 (totality begins), U3 (totality ends), U4 (Moon fully leaves umbra).

flashcard_questions.q: Why does the Moon appear red during a total lunar eclipse?
flashcard_questions.a: Earth's atmosphere refracts and scatters red wavelengths of sunlight into the umbra, illuminating the Moon with a red glow.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are two tidal bulges needed to explain two high tides per day?
flashcard_questions.a: The near-side bulge is caused by the Moon pulling the ocean; the far-side bulge forms because Earth is pulled more than the far-side ocean.
At new moon and full moon, when Moon, Earth and Sun are aligned and tidal effects combine.
At first and last quarter, when the Moon and Sun are at 90° to each other and tidal effects partially cancel.

flashcard_questions.q: Why don't solar eclipses occur at every new moon?
flashcard_questions.a: The Moon's orbit is tilted ~5° to the ecliptic, so the Moon usually passes above or below the Sun at new moon.

flashcard_questions.q: Why can a lunar eclipse be seen from the whole night-side of Earth simultaneously?
flashcard_questions.a: Earth casts its shadow away from the Sun; any observer on the night side has an unobstructed view of the Moon entering that shadow.
The difference in gravitational pull across an extended body — stronger on the near side than the far side.

glossary_terms.definition: The angle subtended by an object at the observer's eye, measuring how large it appears in the sky.
A solar eclipse in which the Moon completely covers the Sun's disc, briefly revealing the solar corona. Observers in the umbra see totality.
A solar eclipse in which the Moon is farther from Earth and appears slightly smaller than the Sun, leaving a ring ('annulus') of sunlight visible around the Moon.
A lunar eclipse in which the Moon passes completely into Earth's umbra, often turning deep red or orange due to refracted sunlight.
The difference in gravitational pull across an extended body — stronger on the near side (facing the source) than on the far side.
Tides of maximum range occurring at new moon and full moon, when the Moon, Earth and Sun are aligned and their tidal effects combine.
Tides of minimum range occurring at first and last quarter, when the Moon and Sun are at right angles to Earth and their tidal effects partially cancel.
The region of complete shadow behind a body where no direct light from the source reaches.
The region of partial shadow surrounding the umbra, where some direct light from the source is still visible.
